summary:
Chile's gender identity law, Law 21.120, has been in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry, without therapy or surgery. Applicants aged 14 to 18 must go before a family court with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and under-14s cannot use the law at all, although it recognises them as transgender.

On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional, in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl. The ruling is confined to that case and does not alter the law's age thresholds generally.

Civil unions have existed since 2015, and marriage and joint adoption have been open to same-sex couples since March 2022. A trans visitor in a relationship that is read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has recourse to marriage. Outright International records that birth certificates carry a third sex option for intersex children.

The 2012 anti-discrimination law, known as the Zamudio Law, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and was extended to gender expression in 2018; hate-crime motivation is an aggravating circumstance in criminal proceedings. A bill criminalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020.

The Migration and Immigration Law, enacted 11 April 2021, bans arbitrary discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and extends protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 allows complementary protection to be granted to asylum seekers who are not recognised, and a foreigner holding complementary protection may not be expelled or returned to a country where their life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk because of, among other grounds, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Article 373 of the Penal Code, which covers offences against morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass gay men, including for holding hands in public. A 2015 Movilh report recorded that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people had been reported, which it credited to the Carabineros human rights department.

Anti-trans violence is documented and has produced emblematic cases. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered and his body hidden for 24 hours; an acquaintance confessed to the killing, which national coverage treats as the emblematic anti-trans homicide case in the country. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour at a hotel in Santiago; the victim described his attacker saying he wanted to kill him.

Institutional discrimination has been litigated. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in April 2025, alleging she was relegated to administrative tasks, that her private life was exposed without her consent and that support was denied.
tangentialFactors:
Movilh's annual assessment, reported in March 2025, judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTQ rights in Chile, citing stalled equality and trans-rights legislation and attributing the failure to advance to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction.

The criminal-law response to anti-LGBT violence runs through aggravating circumstances attached to ordinary offences rather than a standalone incitement or hate-crime offence. A bill criminalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression has passed only the Chamber of Deputies, on 9 January 2020.
localsOnly:
Domestic care access: since 2013, sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy have been financed by the public health system through FONASA. A 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres in the country to call and register transgender people by their social name. The Gender Identity Support Programme, known as PAIG and run under the Crece con Orgullo framework, has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17. In November 2025 Congress removed its funding from the Ministry of Social Development through the 2026 Budget Law; the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres.

Treatment for minors has been contested. In June 2024 the Ministry of Health's Circular 7 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by 7 votes to 3, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.

On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report by 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions. It is not binding and recommends eliminating the Gender Identity Support Programme, restricting the progressive autonomy of minors, banning hormonal treatment for minors, and repealing Circular 812, which protects gender identity in schools.

Rules for trans students in schools come from an April 2017 Ministry of Education circular, Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education, which requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities that respect gender identity, guarantees use of the social name and gender-conforming uniforms, and is sanctionable when not applied. It rests on earlier instruments: the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook ordering non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015-2018 National School Coexistence Policy, which placed the International Day Against Homosexuality and Transphobia in the 2016 school calendar, and the School Inclusion law effective March 2016. Law 21,430, published 15 March 2022, is the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, includes non-discrimination on grounds of sex characteristics and the right to develop a gender identity, and obliges state bodies to create programmes on sexual rights and diversity.

In custody, the national director of Gendarmería signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, covering placement according to assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations; a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives oversees its implementation and the rules for trans visitors' access. Since 2009 the National Organization of Gendarmeries has ended disciplinary sanctions that prevented inmates from dressing according to their gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enactment or rejection of the incitement-to-hatred bill that passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020 is sourced.

No sentence is recorded for the killing of Ever in 2023; the sources establish only that an acquaintance confessed.

Prosecution or conviction figures under the hate-crime aggravating circumstance are not available.

The effect of the Constitutional Court's 9 April 2025 ruling beyond the individual case is unresolved; the wording was declared inapplicable to that case only.

The F&M Global Barometers composite indices, which include a Global Barometer of Transgender Rights, cover Chile, but no scores are available.

Movilh's 24th annual human rights report on sexual and gender diversity (2025) is cited without its findings.

The CEI 57 recommendations are non-binding and no legislative follow-up is sourced.
